Determining hours of UK work

To calculate a seafarer’s UK additional rate (for the purposes of an equivalence declaration) it is necessary to establish their hours of UK work in the pay reference period. The method of calculating hours of UK work is the same for all seafarers, irrespective of the type of work they are doing for the purposes of calculating the total hours of work.

A seafarer’s hours of UK work in a pay reference period can be identified by recording every hour worked, or treated as worked under the Regulations in the UK or its territorial waters.

The hours of work that count as hours of UK work include hours:

when a seafarer is doing UK work

where a seafarer is available, and required to be available, at or near a place of work for the purposes of doing UK work (but not at home). This only includes hours where the seafarer is awake, even if a seafarer by arrangement sleeps onboard the ship and the employer or operator provides suitable facilities for sleeping

spent training when they would otherwise be doing UK work

when a seafarer is travelling, where they would otherwise be doing UK work, unless the travel is between a seafarer’s home or temporary residence and the place of work or a place where an assignment is carried out

For UK work, the time that does not count as working time includes any time spent:

away from work – even if they are paid for that time – including rest breaks, holidays, sick leave, maternity, paternity and adoption leave or industrial action

travelling between home and work (unless the seafarer works whilst travelling) – regardless of whether the seafarer has a fixed place of work

Currency conversion

A seafarer may be paid in a currency other than Great British Pounds (GBPs). In that case, an employer or operator looking to pay the NMWe must make sure that the seafarer’s pay would meet the NMWe hourly rate when converted into GBPs. Employers should assure themselves that they have used a reasonable exchange rate and refer to government exchange rates.

Safe working: tours of duty

A safe working declaration will confirm that on ships providing the service between the UK and France or the UK and the Channel Islands to which the declaration relates, seafarers spend a maximum of:

14 consecutive days working on board

a maximum of 21 days on board if they are undergoing training instead of or as well as working, of which no more than 14 days may be working

Training which is subject to the 21-day maximum includes that for:

the purpose of qualifying as a rating or as an officer

ratings or officers to obtain additional certificates under the Convention on Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping (STCW), 1978, as amended (STCW) under the supervision of another seafarer, while supernumerary

familiarisation with the ship

Time aboard the ship must be immediately followed by at least as many days ashore to rest. For example, if a seafarer works on board a ship for 14 days, this must immediately be followed by at least 14 days of rest ashore.

A period of rest means that the seafarer must not be required by their employer or the operator of the service to work or be available for work, or to be on board a ship. This includes on ships or routes on which the seafarer does not usually work.

The maximum period on board may be exceeded where necessitated by circumstances beyond the control of the operator, the consequences of which could not have been reasonably avoided by the operator. Examples could include:

adverse weather conditions creating vessel delays

travel disruption affecting replacement crew

unforeseen crew sickness

These examples are not exhaustive.

We have supplied examples where operators of services are required to comply with safe working conditions. In some examples it is assumed they have submitted a safe working declaration as required.

Working time examples

Example 1

A member of the crew joins a ship providing a relevant UK-Channel Island service. They must work on board for no more than 14 days before immediately having at least 14 days of rest ashore.

Example 2

A seafarer works aboard a relevant UK-France service for 14 days, after which their employer requires them to work aboard a UK-Belgium service for 14 days without an intervening rest period of at least 14 days. This is not permitted as after working or training aboard a relevant UK-France service the seafarer must immediately have a period of rest ashore of at least an equal number of days, during which they may not be required by their employer or by the operator to work aboard another ship . The operator had provided a safe working declaration to the harbour authority. The operator is guilty of the offence of operating the service inconsistently with a declaration and is liable on summary conviction to a fine.

Training examples

Example 1

A cadet joins a ship operating a relevant UK-France service to gain experience and sea time towards qualifying as an officer, while under the supervision of a crew member. They may spend up to 21 days aboard the ship which must be immediately followed by at least 21 days of rest ashore.

Example 2

An existing officer wants to gain a new STCW certificate. They spend 14 days working aboard the ship in their usual role, then a further 7 days in a supernumerary capacity, under the supervision of another seafarer for the purpose of gaining a new certificate. This must be followed by at least 21 days of rest ashore.

passages.quote:
Introduction

Purpose

The purpose of this guidance is to assist harbour authorities and operators of services in scope of the Seafarers (Wages and Working Conditions) Act 2023 [footnote 1] (“the act”), to comply with their duties under that act, the Seafarers’ Wages Regulations 2024 and the Seafarers (Wages and Working Conditions) Regulations 2026. It also sets out the enforcement powers to be used by the Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) and may assist unions and seafarers to understand how the act and regulations will apply to the payment of wages and working conditions requirements.

Overview

The objective of the legislation is to protect and improve remuneration and safety-related working conditions for seafarers aboard services with close ties to the UK. It makes access to UK harbours for international services calling regularly at a UK port conditional on the provision of declarations confirming that the operator is meeting the standards required by the legislation.

There are different requirements depending on which international port the service comes from.

Requirements for services calling at a UK port at least 120 times a year from a place outside of the UK, except those calling at a port in France or the Channel Islands are set out in the act and the Seafarers’ Wages Regulations 2024. Operators of these services must provide an equivalence declaration which confirms that all seafarers working aboard the service who, because they do not work or ordinarily work in the United Kingdom, are not entitled to the National Minimum Wage, are being paid at least a rate equivalent to it in respect of their work in UK waters.

Requirements for relevant services calling at a port in France or the Channel Islands are set out in the act and the Seafarers (Wages and Working Conditions) Regulations 2026. Operators of these services must provide a:

Remuneration declaration, confirming that all seafarers working aboard the service who are not entitled to the National Minimum Wage because they do not work or ordinarily work in the United Kingdom, are being paid at least a rate equivalent to it for the whole journey.

Safe working declaration, confirming that the service will be operated in accordance with safe working obligations, namely that the maximum period seafarers may spend on board:

14 consecutive days if the seafarer is working during that period

21 consecutive days or the seafarer is undertaking training as well as or instead of working, of which no more than 14 days may be working

Immediately following their time on board they will have a period of rest ashore that is at least the same number of days as they spent on board.

Application

What is a service?

The act applies to services for the carriage of persons or goods by ship, with or without vehicles, between a place outside the United Kingdom and a place in the United Kingdom. This includes services between the UK and the Crown Dependencies. The act therefore does not apply to domestic services. The act also does not apply to a service that is for the purpose of leisure or recreation or to a service provided by a fishing vessel.

The requirement for harbour authorities to request a declaration where a service enters a UK harbour at least 120 times in a relevant year is based on a total number of calls per service, rather than per ship. Multiple ships can be operating the same service. If an operator has more than one ship operating on the same route, this could constitute a single service, and every call made to the UK harbour by any ship operating that service would count towards the 120 times a year.

What constitutes a service will be based on the individual facts of the case. Major factors that should be taken into consideration include the consistency in the product offered to end-users and how it is marketed or made available for booking to the end-user. Examples below are illustrative but not exhaustive.

Examples

Example 1: operator A has 2 passenger ferries operating between Dover and Calais, each making 50 calls at Dover in a relevant year. This would be a single service as it is the same operator performing the same type of passenger service on the same route and would be out of scope as it calls less than 120 times per annum (pa).

Example 2: operator B has one passenger ferry operating the Dover and Calais route and another passenger ferry ship operating between Hull and Rotterdam, each making 100 calls a year. These would be 2 different services, as they are calling at different places outside the UK and both would be out of scope as they each call less than 120 times pa.

Example 3: operator C and operator D are completely separate companies with different brand identities. Both operate passenger ferries between Hull and Rotterdam. Operator C runs 100 times a year and operator D runs 150 time a year. Operator C would not be in scope as it runs fewer than 120 times a year and is a distinct service from that run by operator D. Operator D’s service would be in scope as it calls more than 120 times a year.

Example 4: operator E runs a passenger ferry service X between Dover and Calais which calls 130 times a year. Operator E also runs a lift-on lift off freight service Y which does not carry any passengers. This service calls 80 times a year. These services are separate as they are for different purposes. Service X is in scope but Service Y is not.

Example 5: operator F runs passenger ferries between Dover and Calais. They have 2 vessels operating on this route. Vessel A runs 100 times a year and Vessel B also runs 100 times a year. Vessel A has a bar whereas Vessel B does not. Both vessels are running the same service as they are operating the same route for the same purpose, even if they have slightly different facilities on board. Operator F’s service would in scope as it calls more than 120 times per year.

passages.quote:
usal of access notification can be sent

Where a refusal of access notification is to be given to an operator whose address cannot be ascertained after reasonable inquiry, it may be given by handing it to the master of a ship operating the service.

A refusal of access notification should include the:

Date of the relevant surcharge notification.

Amount of each surcharge in the relevant surcharge notification which has not been paid.

Date and time from which ships providing the service to which the surcharges relate will be refused access to the harbour until the surcharges are paid.

Example

The harbour writes to the operator notifying them of the imposition of surcharges on 1 August.

The operator does not pay the surcharges by 15 September (45 days after imposition of the surcharges). The harbour notifies the operator within the next 5 days that they will refuse ships providing the service access to the harbour if the payment is not made by the deadline of 30 September.

The operator fails to pay the surcharges by the payment deadline. Access is refused until the surcharges are paid.

Notification of non-payment of a surcharge to the Secretary of State

The harbour authority must notify the Secretary of State if a surcharge has been imposed but not paid in the manner specified by the surcharge notification. Notification must include the name of the operator and the date and time from which ships providing the service will be refused access should the surcharge remain unpaid.

Notification must be sent between days 50-55 after the day on which the surcharge notification was sent to the operator to mca.investigations@mcga.gov.uk.

Cancellation of a refusal of access notification

Where an operator makes payment of a surcharge for which a refusal of access notification has been issued, the refusal of access notification in relation to that surcharge is cancelled.

National Minimum Wage equivalent

Overview

The act makes access to UK harbours for international services calling regularly at the UK conditional on paying seafarers a rate at least equivalent to the NMW for their UK work or, in the case of UK-France and UK-Channel Island services their work during the whole journey, or a surcharge. The Regulations specify what constitutes the NMWe rate, as well as setting out the method of calculating the hours that a seafarer is deemed to be working and the hourly rate that they are being paid.

Relationship with the NMW legislation

The regulations use some of the same concepts as the National Minimum Wage Act 1998 and the National Minimum Wages Regulations 2015 (“the NMW legislation”). However, there are important differences between the system established by the regulations and the NMW legislation. In particular, users of the regulations should be aware that some concepts from the NMW legislation are applied in a different way by the regulations.

Calculation of the hourly rate of pay

The main distinction between the NMW legislation and the Regulations concerns the calculation of the hourly rate that seafarers are being paid.

Under the NMW legislation there is a single calculation to determine whether the NMW has been paid: remuneration divided by hours of work. That results in a single hourly rate at which a worker is treated as remunerated.

The method used to assess compliance depends on the service concerned.

Services other than UK-France and UK-Channel Island Services

Under the Seafarers’ Wages Regulations 2024 there are three separate hourly rates, the:

Basic rate: this is essentially the hourly rate received by a seafarer for all of their work before there has been any uplift in pay to meet the NMW equivalent. It is calculated by dividing a seafarer’s basic remuneration by their total hours of work

UK additional rate: this is the hourly rate received by a seafarer which is specific to their hours of work carried out in the UK or its territorial waters (“UK work”). It is calculated by dividing UK additional remuneration (if any) by hours of UK work. UK additional remuneration is any remuneration paid to the seafarer in addition to their basic remuneration in order to meet the requirements of the regulations, for example it only includes remuneration which is attributable to hours of UK work and which would not be paid to the seafarer if the hours of work were not hours of UK work

Overall UK hourly rate: this is the overall hourly rate received by the seafarer for their hours of UK work. It is calculated by adding together their basic rate and their UK additional rate

The regulations and this guidance give much more detail on these concepts. But the following scenario provides a straightforward example of these concepts in practice.

Example: seafarer A (aged 25) works 150 hours a month and their basic remuneration is £1,200. Of the 150 hours, 20 hours a month are hours of UK work.

Seafarer A’s basic rate is £8 an hour (calculated by the sum £1,200 divided by 150 hours).

If the operator of seafarer A’s service wants to provide a declaration under the act, the regulations require that seafarer A be paid the NMWe for their hours of UK work. That is (at the time of publication) £12.71 an hour for a seafarer aged over 21.

To meet this requirement an employer could:

increase seafarer A’s basic rate to £12.71 an hour

pay seafarer A the UK additional rate for their hours of UK work

If the employer decided on the second option then, in this example, the UK additional rate would need to be £4.71. That would result in an overall UK rate of £12.71 (the amount being £8 plus £4.71).

UK-France and UK-Channel Islands Services
